Based on these results, there exists an HTF hot temperature that minimizes the PHX conductance for each PCM salt slurry. For all cases except for the 3-tier PCM, an HTF hot temperature of 715°C minimizes the PHX conductance, which corresponds to the high temperature of the PCM 1 phase change range. For the 3-tier PCM, an HTF hot temperature of 740°C minimizes the PHX conductance. From equation (2), PHX costs scale linearly with conductance. For all cases within this study, the cost of sCO cycle components downstream of 2 the PHX does not change for a given HTF hot temperature. Therefore, PHX conductance directly impacts the total sCO cycle cost, shown in Figure 6. 2 The decrease in PHX conductance is driven by two factors; (i) an increase in temperature differences between the two fluids that occurs during phase change of the PCMs and (ii) a decrease in capacitance ratio between the two fluids because of high heat capacity of the PCM salt slurry during phase change and low salt slurry mass flowrate when phase change is not occurring. Figure 7 and Figure 8 presents an estimate of the temperature difference between the HTF and CO working fluid within the PHX as a function of PHX duty (i.e., cumulative heat 2 transfer). Figure 7 presents the duty-temperature profile for the 3-tier PCM case where the HTF hot temperature is 740°C. Due to the sCO PHX temperature increase being set by the turbine 2 exhaust temperature and the LTR design, the PHX HTF temperature difference is fixed for a given HTF hot temperature. For an HTF hot temperature of 740°C, the HTF temperature difference is approximately 214°C meaning that the HTF exits the PHX at 526°C. At this exit temperature, PCM 3 has entered the phase change region but only utilizes 13% of the assumed temperature range of phase change.
